title: Qualitative Impact Assessment Methods
core_idea: Qualitative impact assessment documents how interventions change people's lives through in-depth interviews, focus groups, and participatory evaluation. Rather than experimental comparison groups, QIA uses narrative evidence and thick description to demonstrate change.

title: Rapid Ethnography and Compressed Fieldwork
core_idea: Rapid ethnography condenses fieldwork into weeks or months instead of the traditional one year or longer. Used in organizational consulting, development work, and humanitarian response, rapid ethnography prioritizes key informants, focused observation, and quick analysis.

title: Reflexivity and Positionality in Research
core_idea: Examines reflexivity and researcher positionality as fundamental to rigorous qualitative research. Covers insider/outsider perspectives, standpoint epistemology, managing power dynamics, and strategies for documenting how researcher characteristics shape data collection and interpretation.

title: Regression Diagnostics: Checking Assumptions and Violations
core_idea: Ordinary least squares regression assumes linearity, homoscedasticity, independence, normality, and no multicollinearity. Real data often violate these.

title: Advanced Regression Discontinuity Design
core_idea: Regression discontinuity design exploits threshold rules in policy assignment to estimate causal effects. When eligibility for treatment depends on crossing a cutoff (income threshold, test score, age), units just above and below the threshold are comparable except for treatment status.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
core_idea: Applies regression discontinuity methods when assignment to treatment depends on a continuous running variable crossing a threshold. Covers sharp and fuzzy RD designs, local polynomial estimation, bandwidth selection, and internal validity advantages of RD for causal inference.

title: Regression Discontinuity: Sharp and Fuzzy Designs
core_idea: Regression discontinuity designs exploit threshold rules in policy or eligibility. When treatment changes discontinuously at a cutoff (sharp RDD) or is affected by a running variable (fuzzy RDD), the discontinuity estimates local treatment effects.

title: Reproducibility and Open Science in Social Research
core_idea: Examines reproducibility and replicability challenges in social science, covering p-hacking, the replication crisis, and solutions including pre-registration, open data, code sharing, and transparent reporting. Addresses tensions between exploratory and confirmatory research.

title: Pre-Registration and Open Science Practices
core_idea: Pre-registration documents analysis plans before data collection or analysis, reducing researcher degrees of freedom and distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory analyses. Open science practices—sharing code, data, materials, and preprints—enable reproduction and verification.

title: Advanced Research Design
core_idea: Synthesizes research design architecture for complex social investigations, covering problem formulation, literature integration, hypothesis development, and strategic selection among quantitative, qualitative, and mixed approaches. Emphasizes alignment between research questions and design choices.

title: Research Design: From Questions to Methods
core_idea: Sound research design bridges theory and evidence by specifying research questions, hypotheses, populations, and methods. Strong designs anticipate validity threats and clarify how data collection and analysis answer the research question.

title: Research Ethics in Social Science
core_idea: Covers ethical principles governing human subjects research: informed consent, confidentiality, minimizing harm, and justice. Examines institutional review processes, special considerations for vulnerable populations, and emerging challenges in digital/digital ethnography and secondary data research

title: Research Integrity and Open Science: Transparency and Reproducibility
core_idea: Research integrity requires transparency about methods, data, and decisions. Open science practices—preregistration, data sharing, code availability—reduce researcher degrees of freedom and enable replication.

title: Sampling Strategies in Social Research

title: Sensitivity Analysis: Robustness to Unmeasured Confounding
core_idea: All observational causal estimates depend on unverifiable assumptions about unmeasured confounders. Sensitivity analysis quantifies how large unmeasured confounding must be to overturn conclusions.

title: Computational Simulation of Social Systems

title: Social Network Analysis
core_idea: Introduces network analysis as both theory and method for studying social relationships, structures, and flows. title: Structural Equation Modeling with Latent Variables
core_idea: Introduces SEM as a comprehensive framework for testing theories with latent variables and indirect effects. Covers path analysis, measurement models, structural models, and model fit assessment.

title: Advanced Survey Design
core_idea: Addresses design of effective surveys for social research, covering question construction, response option design, scale development, survey modes (paper, online, phone), non-response bias, and data collection best practices. Emphasizes reducing response and coverage error.

title: Survival Analysis and Event History Methods
core_idea: Event history methods analyze timing of social events—divorce, job transitions, political regime changes. These methods handle censoring (incomplete observation periods) and allow time-varying covariates.

title: Synthetic Control Methods
core_idea: Synthetic control constructs a counterfactual for a treated unit by taking a weighted combination of untreated units. When a single unit (country, region, organization) experiences an intervention, its pre-intervention trends may not match any single control unit, but a weighted average may.

title: Computational Text Analysis for Social Data
core_idea: Computational text analysis uses algorithms to extract patterns, themes, and meanings from large text corpora—news articles, social media, interviews, historical documents. Methods range from counting word frequencies and calculating sentiment to unsupervised topic modeling and supervised classifica

title: Time Series Cross-Section (TSCS) Models
core_idea: TSCS data combines the temporal dimension (many time periods) with the cross-sectional dimension (many units like countries or organizations), creating a grid of observations. TSCS models account for complex dependence structures: within-unit autocorrelation, contemporaneous correlation across units

title: Time Series Analysis of Social Phenomena
core_idea: Extends regression methods to analyze temporal social data with autocorrelation. Covers autoregressive models, moving averages, testing for stationarity, and interrupted time series designs for evaluating policy interventions.

title: Triangulation: Convergent Validity and Method Confirmation
core_idea: Triangulation uses multiple methods, data sources, or investigators to examine questions from different angles. Convergent findings increase confidence; divergence prompts investigation.

title: Validity: Construct, Internal, External, and Statistical
core_idea: Validity concerns whether we measure what we claim (construct validity), whether observed associations reflect causal effects (internal validity), and whether findings generalize (external validity). Each type faces distinct threats, and research trade-offs often exist between them.

title: Vector Autoregression (VAR) Models
core_idea: Vector autoregression models capture dynamic interdependencies among multiple time series. Each variable is regressed on its own past values and the past values of all other variables.

title: Visual and Multimodal Ethnography
core_idea: Visual ethnography uses photographs, video, and visual analysis as primary data collection and representation methods. Multimodal ethnography integrates visual, aural, and textual data to capture embodied, sensory social practices.

title: The Agency-Structure Problem
core_idea: The agency-structure problem asks: are human actions determined by social structures (determinism) or are humans free agents who create structures (voluntarism)? Sociological theory must account for both.

title: Alienation in Capitalist Society
core_idea: Marx identified alienation as workers' estrangement from the products of their labor, from the labor process itself, from their human essence, and from each other. Under capitalism, workers sell their labor-power as a commodity, losing control over what they produce and how they produce it.

title: Anomie and Social Integration
core_idea: Anomie is a state of normlessness or moral deregulation in which individuals lack clear social guidelines for behavior. Durkheim linked anomie to rapid social change, economic crises, and social disconnection, arguing suicide rates spike during anomic periods.

title: Anthony Giddens and Structuration Theory
core_idea: Structuration theory resolves the structure-agency problem by arguing they are mutually constitutive: structures (rules and resources) enable and constrain human action, while action reproduces and potentially transforms structures. Social actors possess knowledgeability and reflexivity; they contin

title: Authority and Domination in Sociology
core_idea: Authority is power perceived as legitimate; domination is power exercised over others. Weber identified three types of authority (traditional, charismatic, rational-legal).

title: Bourdieu: Cultural Capital and Social Reproduction

Those raised in cultured families gain embodied cultural capital (manners, speech) that education institutions reward, disguising advantage as me

title: Bourdieu: Field and Social Space
core_idea: A field is a structured social space (art world, science, politics, education) where agents compete for authority and resources according to field-specific rules. Positions in a field depend on capital (economic, cultural, social, symbolic).

title: Bourdieu: Habitus and Dispositions

title: Bureaucracy and Organizational Structure

Bureaucracy maximizes efficiency but may suppress individual a

title: Class Struggle and Class Consciousness
core_idea: Marx argued that society is fundamentally divided between classes defined by their relationship to the means of production. Class struggle between bourgeoisie and proletariat is the engine of historical change.

title: Class Struggle and Historical Change
core_idea: Marx argued that history is driven by class struggle—the conflict between owners of the means of production and those who must sell their labor. Each historical epoch is defined by its dominant mode of production and corresponding class conflict.

title: Coercion and Social Domination
core_idea: Conflict theory emphasizes that social order is maintained not through consensus but through coercion and power differentials. Those with power enforce rules that protect their interests, and social order reflects the interests of the dominant class or group.

title: Auguste Comte and Positivism in Sociology
core_idea: Auguste Comte founded sociology as a positive science studying society through empirical observation rather than philosophy. He proposed a hierarchy of sciences and viewed society as evolving through theological, metaphysical, and positive stages.

title: Conflict Theory in Sociology
core_idea: Conflict theory emphasizes that society is characterized by inequality and competition over scarce resources. Different groups (classes, races, genders) have conflicting interests; social order is maintained through coercion and the power of dominant groups, not consensus or shared values.

title: Cultural Capital and Social Inequality

title: Cultural Reproduction and Educational Systems

title: The Culture Industry
core_idea: Adorno and Horkheimer's concept of the culture industry describes how mass media and entertainment function as systems of ideological control. The culture industry produces standardized, formulaic content that pacifies audiences and makes them docile consumers.

title: Dialectical Materialism

title: The Division of Labor and Social Cohesion
core_idea: For Durkheim, the division of labor is the primary cause of the transition from mechanical to organic solidarity and a fundamental source of social integration in modern societies. However, the division of labor produces social cohesion only when properly regulated.

title: Anomie and Social Solidarity
core_idea: Anomie is a state of normlessness where social solidarity breaks down and individuals lack moral regulation. It arises during rapid social change when old norms collapse before new ones form.

title: Durkheim's Concept of Collective Consciousness
core_idea: Durkheim defined the collective consciousness as the shared beliefs, values, and moral rules that bind a society together. It exists beyond any individual and exerts coercive force on them.

title: Mechanical and Organic Solidarity

title: Durkheim and Social Facts
core_idea: Émile Durkheim defined social facts as ways of acting, thinking, and feeling external to individuals and exerting coercive power over them. Language, law, and norms are social facts—they're collective phenomena that constrain individuals yet enable society.

title: Émile Durkheim and Social Facts
core_idea: Durkheim defined social facts as collective phenomena (norms, institutions, beliefs, laws) that exist independently of any individual and exert coercive force on behavior. Social facts must be studied empirically as things, not derived from individual psychology.

title: Erving Goffman and Dramaturgy
core_idea: Goffman analyzed social interaction as theatrical performance: individuals manage impressions ('front stage' behavior vs. 'back stage' authenticity), perform roles, and collaborate with others to maintain shared definitions of situations.

title: Ethnomethodology
core_idea: Ethnomethodology studies how people continuously accomplish social order through mundane practices and talk. Rather than assuming society is a stable structure, it asks: how do people collaboratively produce recognizable social situations?

title: Feminist Sociology and Intersectionality

title: Feminist Sociology
core_idea: Feminist sociology challenges male-dominated theories by centering gender as a primary axis of inequality. It examines how patriarchal structures permeate institutions, shaping access to power, resources, and knowledge production.

title: Biopolitics and Population Governance
core_idea: Foucault's concept of biopolitics describes how modern power has increasingly come to manage life itself at the population level—health, sexuality, fertility, mortality. Governments regulate populations through public health, medicine, sexuality policies, and eugenics.

title: Discipline and Surveillance
core_idea: Foucault analyzed how modern power operates through discipline rather than mere repression. The panopticon—a prison design where inmates cannot know if they are watched—exemplifies disciplinary power: constant possible surveillance produces self-regulation.

title: Genealogy as Historical Method
core_idea: Foucault's genealogical method investigates the historical emergence of concepts and practices that seem natural or inevitable, revealing instead how they were contingently constructed through power relations. Genealogy traces ruptures and discontinuities rather than linear progress.

title: Foucault and Power-Knowledge in Sociology
core_idea: Foucault analyzed how power and knowledge are inseparable: knowledge is always produced within power relations, and power operates through knowledge. title: Foucault: Power, Knowledge, and Discourse
core_idea: Foucault reconceptualized power not as possession but as productive relations operating through discourse and institutions. Knowledge and power are inseparable: what counts as truth is established through power relations and simultaneously produces subjects.

title: The Frankfurt School and Critical Theory
core_idea: The Frankfurt School (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse) extended Marxism to analyze how advanced capitalism perpetuates domination through culture, media, and ideology rather than just economic coercion. They examined how the culture industry manufactures consent and forecloses critical thinking.

title: George Herbert Mead and Social Interaction
core_idea: Mead argued that mind and self are not innate but emerge through social interaction. Through 'taking the role of the other,' children develop a sense of self by imagining how others perceive them.

title: George Herbert Mead and the Social Self
core_idea: Mead argued that mind and self emerge through social interaction. The self develops through role-taking and internalizing the generalized other (society's attitudes).

title: Erving Goffman and Dramaturgy
core_idea: Goffman analyzes social interaction as theatrical performance. People manage impressions through front-stage behavior (public) and backstage behavior (private), using props, costumes, and scripts.

title: Granovetter and Network Theory
core_idea: Network theory analyzes society as patterns of connections between actors. Granovetter showed that weak ties (distant acquaintances) often transmit novel information better than strong ties (close friends), solving the embeddedness problem.

title: Granovetter and the Strength of Weak Ties

title: Jürgen Habermas and Communicative Action

title: Ideal Types as Sociological Tools
core_idea: An ideal type is a conceptual tool that exaggerates or highlights certain features of a phenomenon to make analysis possible. It is not a moral or practical ideal but an abstract analytical construct.

title: Institutional Theory in Sociology
core_idea: New institutional theory studies how institutions gain legitimacy and persist through isomorphism (conformity to norms) rather than efficiency alone. Institutions are social rules constraining behavior; organizations adopt practices for legitimacy even if inefficient.

title: Critique of Instrumental Rationality
core_idea: Critical theory critiques instrumental rationality—the reduction of all reasoning to calculation of means toward given ends. This rationality dominates modern societies, treating nature, others, and even human relationships as resources to be optimized.

title: Intersectionality in Sociological Analysis
core_idea: Intersectionality examines how multiple systems of oppression (gender, race, class, sexuality, disability) interact in ways that can't be reduced to sum of individual oppressions. An individual's position results from simultaneous location in multiple hierarchies.

title: Introduction to Sociology
core_idea: Sociology is the systematic study of human societies, social institutions, and patterns of human behavior within groups and organizations. It bridges the individual and society by examining how social structures shape behavior while individuals collectively create and recreate those structures.

title: Karl Marx and Historical Materialism

Societies progress through stages (primitive communism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism, socialism) determined by changes in how goods

title: Weber's Types of Legitimate Authority
core_idea: Weber identified three ideal types of legitimate authority: traditional (based on custom and inheritance), charismatic (based on personal magnetism and claimed special powers), and rational-legal (based on formal rules and expertise). title: The Looking-Glass Self
core_idea: Cooley's concept of the looking-glass self describes how we develop our sense of self by imagining how we appear to others, imagining their judgment, and developing self-feeling in response. The self is socially constructed through interaction: we see ourselves reflected in others' reactions to us.

title: Manifest and Latent Functions

title: Marx and Historical Materialism
core_idea: Historical materialism posits that material conditions and economic relations—not ideas or great individuals—drive social change. Society evolves through class struggle as productive forces outgrow existing relations of production.

title: Alienation in Marxist Theory
core_idea: Alienation describes how capitalism separates workers from the products of their labor, from the labor process itself, from their species-being, and from each other. Workers become commodities, their creativity is stolen, and labor becomes instrumental suffering rather than self-expression.

title: Marx's Base and Superstructure Model

title: Max Weber and Rationalization in Modernity
core_idea: Weber identified rationalization as the defining process of modernity: the replacement of traditional and affectual action with instrumental, calculative reasoning. title: Mechanical and Organic Solidarity
core_idea: Durkheim distinguished mechanical solidarity (traditional societies bound by shared beliefs, rituals, and undifferentiated labor) from organic solidarity (modern societies bound by functional interdependence and specialized division of labor). Modernization involves this structural transition.

title: Network Analysis in Sociology
core_idea: Network analysis studies social structure as patterns of connections between actors (individuals, organizations, nations). Sociologists examine centrality, clustering, brokerage, and diffusion to understand how networks constrain opportunity, transmit information, and shape outcomes.

title: Talcott Parsons and Systems Theory

title: Phenomenological Sociology
core_idea: Phenomenological sociology focuses on how people experience and interpret their lived world. It examines consciousness, intentionality, and the structures of everyday experience.

title: Pierre Bourdieu: Habitus and Field
core_idea: Bourdieu's theory integrates micro and macro levels through habitus (internalized social structures and dispositions) and field (structured social space with unequal distribution of capital). Individuals navigate fields based on habitus; their success depends on possessing the right forms of capital

title: Postcolonial Sociology
core_idea: Postcolonial sociology examines how colonialism shaped societies and persists after formal decolonization through cultural imperialism, economic dependency, and psychological domination. title: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
core_idea: Weber's famous thesis argued that Calvinist Protestant ethics—emphasizing worldly diligence, frugal living, and proving salvation through economic success—created psychological conditions favorable to capitalism's emergence and development.

title: The Protestant Work Ethic and Capitalism

title: Rational Choice Theory in Sociology
core_idea: Rational choice theory models social behavior as utility-maximization: individuals calculate costs/benefits and act in self-interest. It explains cooperation (reciprocal exchange), markets (supply/demand), collective action (free-riding problems).

title: Reflexivity and Late Modernity
core_idea: Giddens argues that modernity is characterized by reflexivity—the continuous monitoring and revision of social practices based on incoming knowledge about them. Unlike traditional societies where practices are justified by precedent, modern individuals must continually decide how to live and what to

title: Robert Merton and Functional Analysis
core_idea: Merton refined functionalism by distinguishing manifest functions (intended, recognized consequences) from latent functions (unintended, unrecognized consequences). He identified dysfunctions (consequences that harm social integration) and rejected the assumption that all social phenomena are functi

title: Robert K. Merton: Manifest and Latent Functions
core_idea: Merton distinguished manifest functions (intended, recognized consequences of social practices) from latent functions (unintended, unrecognized consequences). He also introduced dysfunction—consequences that disrupt system equilibrium.

title: Role-Taking and Self-Development
core_idea: Mead argued that humans develop consciousness and selfhood through role-taking—the ability to imagine ourselves in others' positions and anticipate their responses. Self-awareness emerges through language and symbolic communication, allowing us to take the attitude of others toward ourselves.

title: Self and Identity in Social Interaction
core_idea: The self is not a fixed essence but a dynamic product of social interaction. Identity is multiple, context-dependent, and continuously negotiated in interaction with others.

title: Social Capital and Network Resources
core_idea: Social capital refers to resources available through social networks and relationships based on trust and reciprocity. Individuals and groups with stronger networks and higher-status connections gain access to information, opportunities, and support that facilitate success.

title: Social Dysfunction in Functionalist Analysis
core_idea: Functionalism recognizes that some practices and institutions can have dysfunctional consequences that undermine system stability. Dysfunctions are unintended negative effects that weaken integration or prevent adaptation.

title: The Sociological Imagination
core_idea: C. Wright Mills's concept of the sociological imagination is the ability to connect personal troubles to public issues and to see how biography and history intersect within society.

title: Sociology of Knowledge
core_idea: Sociology of knowledge examines how social structures shape what is known and how knowledge is produced, validated, and distributed. It investigates what counts as legitimate knowledge in different contexts and how power relations influence knowledge production.

title: Structural Functionalism
core_idea: Structural functionalism views society as a system of interconnected parts (institutions, norms, roles) that function to maintain social stability and integration. Each part serves functions for the whole; social change occurs to restore equilibrium when dysfunctions arise.

title: Giddens: Structuration Theory
core_idea: Structuration theory overcomes the agency/structure divide: structures enable and constrain action; actions reproduce and transform structures. Structures exist as rules and resources that agents recursively draw on, and through this recursive process, structures persist or change.

title: Suicide as a Social Fact: Durkheim's Empirical Study

title: Surplus Value and Labor Exploitation

title: Symbolic Interactionism: Foundations
core_idea: Symbolic interactionism posits that humans act based on meanings they assign to things, and these meanings arise from social interaction. People continuously interpret and re-interpret the world, creating and modifying meanings through social processes.

title: Symbolic Interactionism
core_idea: Symbolic interactionism views society as emerging from face-to-face interactions where people create meaning through symbols and language. Humans act based on meanings they assign to things; these meanings arise from interaction and are modified through interpretation.

title: Symbolic Violence
core_idea: Bourdieu defines symbolic violence as domination that is exercised through misrepresentation and that appears legitimate to both dominators and the dominated. Symbolic violence works through cultural meanings and practices that make unequal relations seem natural or deserved.

title: Talcott Parsons and Action Systems Theory
core_idea: Parsons developed a comprehensive systems theory in which social action is organized through four functional imperatives: adaptation (economic), goal-attainment (political), integration (social), and latency (cultural). These functions must be performed for any system to survive.

title: Theories and Paradigms in Sociology

title: Wallerstein and World-Systems Theory
core_idea: World-systems theory views capitalism as a global system with hierarchical division: core (wealthy, industrialized), periphery (colonized, extractive), semi-periphery (intermediate). This structure, not national culture, determines development paths.

title: Weber's Ideal Type of Bureaucracy
core_idea: Weber's ideal type of bureaucracy exhibits hierarchy, written rules, impersonal relationships, specialized roles, and merit-based hiring. It's the most efficient form of administration but creates rigidity, goal displacement, and alienation.

title: Weber and the Iron Cage of Rationalization
core_idea: Max Weber identified rationalization—the replacement of tradition and emotion with calculation and efficiency—as modernity's defining feature. Institutions increasingly organize around instrumental rationality (means-to-ends calculation) rather than value rationality.

title: Weber's Types of Social Action

title: World-Systems Theory
core_idea: Wallerstein's world-systems theory analyzes global inequality as produced by a capitalist world-system divided into core (developed) nations, periphery (developing) nations, and semi-periphery. title: Achieved versus Ascribed Status and Social Position

title: Aging and Society: Gerontological Perspectives
core_idea: How societies treat aging and older people reveals cultural values and structural inequalities. Age stratification systems distribute material resources, status, and opportunities based on age.

title: Applied Sociology and Program Evaluation
core_idea: Applied sociology uses sociological knowledge, research methods, and theory to address real-world social issues. Program evaluation research asks whether interventions achieve their intended goals and for whom.

title: Boundary Work and Status Maintenance
core_idea: Groups maintain their status through boundary work—defining symbolic boundaries that separate them from lower-status groups. These cultural distinctions in taste, language, education, and lifestyle become markers of group membership.

title: Caste, Class, and Estate Systems of Stratification

title: Collective Behavior and Crowds
core_idea: Collective behavior refers to relatively spontaneous and unstructured actions by a group in response to a shared situation—crowds, panics, fads, crazes, and rumors. title: Collective Effervescence and Solidarity Rituals
core_idea: Durkheim argued that rituals create collective effervescence—heightened emotional energy—that bonds group members and reinforces shared values. title: Community and Social Bonds: Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft
core_idea: Community (Gemeinschaft) refers to groups united by place, shared interests, or deep social ties with intimate, face-to-face bonds and mutual obligation. Society (Gesellschaft) emphasizes formal, impersonal relationships based on contracts and instrumental interests.

title: Credential Inflation and Educational Expansion
core_idea: As educational credentials become widespread, their market value declines, pushing individuals and institutions to pursue ever-higher credentials. This educational arms race increases total human capital investment without increasing the rate of upward social mobility.

title: Criminology: A Sociological Approach
core_idea: Sociological criminology views crime not as individual pathology or moral failure but as behavior shaped by social structures, strain, opportunity, and labeling processes. title: Cultural Diversity and Pluralism in Society
core_idea: Multicultural or plural societies contain multiple distinct cultural groups with different values and practices. title: Cultural Transmission and Intergenerational Continuity
core_idea: Societies reproduce themselves by transmitting cultural knowledge, values, practices, and traditions across generations. Families, schools, and institutions serve as transmission mechanisms, socializing younger generations into existing patterns.

title: Culture and Society
core_idea: Culture encompasses the shared beliefs, values, norms, symbols, language, and material objects that members of a society use to make sense of their world and coordinate action. title: Demographic Structure and Population Effects

title: Deviance and Social Control
core_idea: Deviance refers to behaviors, beliefs, or conditions that violate social norms and invite negative social reactions. It is not an intrinsic property of acts but a product of social definition — what counts as deviant varies by culture, context, and historical period.

title: Education as a Social Institution
core_idea: Education systems perform multiple functions: transmitting knowledge and skills, socializing children into cultural norms, sorting individuals into occupational roles, and legitimating social hierarchies. Functionalists emphasize meritocracy — education allocates rewards based on ability and effort.

title: Family as a Social Institution
core_idea: The family is a central social institution that organizes reproduction, primary socialization, emotional support, and the intergenerational transmission of resources and identity. title: Formal Organizations: Structure and Function
core_idea: Formal organizations are deliberately structured to accomplish specific goals through roles, rules, and hierarchies. They exist across institutional spheres and reveal how rules, incentives, and authority shape behavior and outcomes in ways that extend beyond individual preferences.

title: Gender, Sex, and Sexuality
core_idea: Sociology distinguishes sex (biological characteristics associated with male/female bodies) from gender (socially constructed roles, behaviors, and identities culturally associated with masculinity and femininity). title: Gender: Socialization, Performance, and Inequality
core_idea: Gender is learned through socialization and continuously performed through interaction, not determined by biology alone. Gender inequality is maintained through institutional practices and cultural norms that systematically advantage men over women in access to resources, authority, and status.

title: Generational Differences and Cohort Effects

title: Globalization and Society

title: Group Dynamics and Conformity Pressure

title: In-Groups, Out-Groups, and Social Boundaries
core_idea: People distinguish between in-groups and out-groups, often viewing their own group more favorably. This boundary-marking serves identity functions but can fuel intergroup conflict, prejudice, and the basis for systematic discrimination and inequality.

title: In-Group and Out-Group Identity
core_idea: Humans naturally categorize themselves and others into 'us' versus 'them' groups. Membership in an in-group strengthens identity and belonging, but simultaneously can trigger favoritism toward the in-group and prejudice against out-groups.

title: Industrialization and Social Transformation
core_idea: Industrialization restructured society profoundly: moving populations from rural to urban areas, replacing extended families with nuclear families, shifting labor to formal organizations, and creating new class structures based on capital rather than land ownership.

title: Institutional Change and Transformation
core_idea: Institutions are relatively stable patterns and rules that structure social life, but they are not static. Institutional change occurs through innovation, diffusion of new practices, crises that delegitimize existing arrangements, or deliberate reform movements.

title: Institutional Isomorphism and Organizational Conformity

title: Institutional Legitimacy and Compliance

title: Institutionalization Processes and Routinization

title: Intersectionality

title: Labeling Theory and Secondary Deviance
core_idea: Labeling theory argues that deviance is not an intrinsic property of an act but a consequence of social labeling and reaction. Once labeled as deviant, individuals may internalize this identity and commit secondary deviance—acts committed as a response to being labeled.

title: The Life Course Perspective
core_idea: The life course perspective views individuals as moving through socially defined life stages (childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age), each with distinct expectations, opportunities, and constraints. title: The Meritocracy Myth and Educational Sorting
core_idea: The meritocracy myth claims success derives from individual talent and effort rather than inherited advantage. Educational systems systematically advantage already-privileged groups through cultural capital, social networks, and subtle selection mechanisms.

title: Micro and Macro Sociology: Levels of Analysis

title: Microsociology and Everyday Interaction
core_idea: Microsociology focuses on small-scale social interaction in everyday life—how people manage impressions, negotiate meanings, define situations, and sustain social order in face-to-face encounters. Seemingly trivial everyday interactions encode larger patterns about power, status, gender, and culture

title: Moral Panic and Amplification Spirals
core_idea: A moral panic occurs when media, elites, and public opinion amplify concern about a perceived threat disproportionate to actual risk. The amplification process itself increases the deviant behavior being condemned, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy.

title: Occupational Closure and Professional Monopoly
core_idea: Occupational closure describes how professional and occupational groups restrict entry to preserve high status and earnings through credentialing requirements, licensing, and gatekeeping. This exclusion maintains inequality between insiders and outsiders and limits social mobility from below.

title: Occupational Prestige and Status Systems
core_idea: Occupations rank in a hierarchy of prestige and rewards based on income, education required, and social esteem. Prestige rankings are relatively stable and reflect cultural values.

title: Organizational Culture and Member Identity
core_idea: Organizations develop distinctive cultures—shared norms, values, and symbols—that persist across members and shape behavior. Members are socialized into organizational roles and identities, often internalizing organizational values.

title: Organized Crime and Criminal Subcultures
core_idea: Criminal subcultures develop their own norms, codes of conduct, and social hierarchies. Members are socialized into deviant roles and identities through interaction with other deviants.

title: Power, Authority, and Legitimacy
core_idea: Power, in Max Weber's classic definition, is the ability to achieve one's ends even against resistance. Authority is legitimate power — power that is recognized as rightful by those subject to it.

title: Primary Groups and Intimate Relationships
core_idea: Primary groups are small, intimate, face-to-face groups such as families and close friendships where relationships are personal and valued for their own sake. These groups powerfully shape identity and behavior through emotional bonds and continuous interaction.

title: Primary and Secondary Groups
core_idea: Groups exist on a spectrum from primary groups characterized by intimate, personal, long-term relationships (families, friend circles) to secondary groups that are formal, instrumental, and task-focused (workplaces, organizations). title: Protest Movements and Social Activism
core_idea: Protest movements mobilize people around grievances and demands for social change through collective action. Successful movements require organizational structure, leadership, strategic framing, and resources.

title: Race and Ethnicity
core_idea: Race is a social construct—a system of classification based on perceived physical differences (especially skin color) that societies have invested with social meaning and used to distribute resources, rights, and opportunities unequally. title: Race, Ethnicity, and Social Inequality
core_idea: Race and ethnicity are socially constructed categories shaped by power and history, not biological realities. Racial and ethnic inequality persists through institutional discrimination, prejudice, and structural barriers that concentrate opportunity and disadvantage across generations.

title: Reference Groups and Social Comparison
core_idea: People evaluate themselves by comparing their status and abilities to reference groups—groups used as standards for self-evaluation. These may be membership groups or aspirational groups.

title: Relative Deprivation and Social Discontent
core_idea: Relative deprivation is the perception that one's group is unfairly disadvantaged compared to reference groups or past expectations. Discontent arises not from absolute deprivation but from the gap between expectations and actual conditions.

title: Relative Rewards, Income Inequality, and Aspiration Spirals
core_idea: When income inequality increases even if absolute living standards rise, people's aspirations rise faster, creating perceived deprivation. This aspiration spiral can fuel social unrest during periods of economic growth if inequality is worsening.

title: Religion and Society
core_idea: Sociology of religion examines religion as a social phenomenon—how it creates community, legitimates power, provides meaning, and sometimes motivates social change. Durkheim argued that religion's true function is social: the sacred/profane distinction reinforces collective identity and solidarity.

title: Resocialization and Adult Identity Transformation
core_idea: Resocialization is learning new roles and identities in adulthood—becoming a parent, entering a profession, adapting to illness or incarceration. title: Resource Mobilization and Collective Action Theory
core_idea: Resource mobilization theory explains how social movements succeed: they require money, volunteers, communication networks, and access to media and political institutions. title: Secondary Groups and Formal Organization
core_idea: Secondary groups are larger, impersonal formal organizations where relationships are instrumental and role-based. Members interact to achieve specific goals rather than for intrinsic enjoyment, making these groups more replaceable and less emotionally binding than primary groups.

title: Secondary Socialization and Resocialization in Adulthood
core_idea: While primary socialization in childhood is foundational, secondary socialization continues throughout adulthood as individuals enter new roles and institutions. Adults learn new norms, values, and identities through occupational socialization, marriage, parenthood, and major life transitions.

title: Social Change and Modernization
core_idea: Social change refers to shifts in social structures and cultural patterns over time. Modernization theory traces change from traditional to modern societies, involving urbanization, industrialization, and rationalization.

title: Social Influence Mechanisms: Obedience, Compliance, and Conformity
core_idea: Social influence operates through several distinct mechanisms: obedience (compliance with explicit commands from authority), conformity (alignment with group norms), and compliance (yielding to direct requests). These mechanisms are essential for coordinating behavior and transmitting cultural value

title: Social Institutions
core_idea: Social institutions are enduring, organized systems of norms, roles, and relationships that fulfill basic social needs and reproduce social order across generations. Major institutions include the family, education, religion, economy, and government (polity).

title: Social Mobility and Life Chances
core_idea: Social mobility refers to movement between social classes across generations. Life chances—access to education, jobs, and health—are distributed unequally by class, race, and family background.

title: Social Movements
core_idea: Social movements are sustained collective efforts to promote or resist social change, distinguished from collective behavior by their organization, duration, and strategic orientation. title: Social Norms, Values, and Sanctions
core_idea: Social norms are shared expectations about appropriate behavior in given situations. They range from folkways (informal, weakly enforced customs like table manners) to mores (strongly held moral norms) to taboos (absolute prohibitions).

title: Sociological Frameworks for Understanding Social Problems
core_idea: A sociological approach to social problems emphasizes that problems are socially defined rather than objectively present—different groups contest what counts as a problem and what causes it. title: Social Stratification

title: Social Structure and Agency
core_idea: Social structure refers to the recurring patterned arrangements—norms, roles, institutions, hierarchies—that constrain and enable behavior across a society. Agency refers to the capacity of individuals to act independently and make choices.

title: Socialization
core_idea: Socialization is the lifelong process through which individuals learn the norms, values, behaviors, and social skills appropriate to their society and particular social positions within it. title: The Sociological Imagination
core_idea: The sociological imagination, a concept developed by C. Wright Mills, is the capacity to see the relationship between individual experience and larger social forces.

title: The Sociological Perspective: Core Principles

title: Research Methods in Sociology

title: The Sociology of Economy and Markets
core_idea: Economic sociology studies the social structures and institutions that shape economic behavior and outcomes. Markets are not natural, self-regulating mechanisms but are embedded in social norms, networks, trust relations, and power dynamics.

title: The Sociology of Politics
core_idea: Political sociology examines how social structures shape political behavior, institutions, and power. title: The Sociology of Work and Occupations
core_idea: Work is not merely an economic activity but a social institution that shapes identity, status, and daily social relationships. title: Status Attainment and Occupational Mobility
core_idea: Status attainment research models how individuals achieve their social position through education, occupational choice, and family background. Parental socioeconomic status strongly influences children's educational attainment, which then affects their occupational status and earnings.

title: Status, Honor, and Prestige Systems
core_idea: Status systems rank individuals and groups by honor and prestige based on culturally valued characteristics. Unlike economic resources or power, prestige is not zero-sum and depends entirely on collective agreement about what deserves respect.

title: Status Inconsistency and Cognitive Strain
core_idea: Status inconsistency occurs when individuals rank high on some stratification dimensions but low on others—highly educated with low income, or wealthy in a society that devalues their ethnicity. This inconsistency creates psychological strain because people expect consistency in status dimensions.

title: Subcultures and Countercultures
core_idea: Subcultures are groups that share distinct values, norms, and practices that differ from mainstream culture while remaining part of the broader society (examples: academic disciplines, hobbyist communities, professional groups). Countercultures actively challenge and reject dominant cultural values.

title: Total Institutions and Resocialization

title: Types of Societies and Societal Evolution
core_idea: Sociologists classify societies by subsistence technology: hunting-gathering, pastoral, horticultural, agrarian, and industrial. Each type has distinct features regarding inequality, family structure, and authority.

title: Urbanization and Urban Life
core_idea: Urbanization—the increasing concentration of populations in cities—is one of the defining social transformations of modernity. Urban sociologists study how city life shapes social relationships, identity, and community.

title: Urbanization and Urban Social Life
core_idea: Urbanization concentrates large, diverse populations in cities, creating unique social patterns: anonymity, weak ties, and impersonal interactions. Cities offer opportunity but also social problems like crime and housing inequality—effects that vary by neighborhood and residents' social class.

title: White-Collar Crime and Organizational Deviance
